papers.title: Efficacy, safety, and tolerability of inhaled levodopa (CVT-301) across age, timing of motor fluctuations, and treatment initiation in Parkinson's disease: Pooled analysis of three phase 3 trials.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Most people with Parkinson's disease (PwP) eventually develop motor response fluctuations (OFF episodes) a few years after starting oral levodopa. CVT-301 is an inhaled levodopa formulation developed to alleviate OFF episodes. AIM: Assess the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of CVT-301 across subgroups by age and timing of treatment initiation using data from phase 3 clinical trials. METHODS: This post hoc analysis pooled data from three phase 3 trials (CVT-301-004, CVT-301-005, and CVT-301-004E) involving PwP experiencing OFF episodes. Efficacy endpoints included the change in Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale Part III (UPDRS-III) score from pre-dose to 30 min post-dose at week 12. Analyses were conducted across age subgroups (<55, 55-64, 65-74, ≥75 years at diagnosis and during study treatment) and timing of treatment initiation (early [<2 years] versus late [≥2 years]) in relation to the first OFF episode. Safety assessments focused on treatment-related cough and throat irritation. RESULTS: Data from 437 PwP were pooled. Mean (standard deviation [SD]) improvement in UPDRS-III score ranged from 5.7 (9.0) points in patients aged ≥75 years at diagnosis to 16.4 (13.8) points in those aged <55 years at study treatment initiation. Mean (SD) improvement in UPDRS-III score was 14.6 (12.0) and 14.7 (10.1) points in the early and late treatment initiation groups, respectively. Treatment-related cough (17.2%) and throat irritation (3.0%) were predominantly mild, transient, and rarely led to treatment modification. CONCLUSIONS: CVT-301 demonstrated consistent efficacy and favorable tolerability across the age and treatment-initiation subgroups evaluated in this analysis.

papers.title: Ultrasensitive detection of alpha-synuclein oligomers in human plasma using optimized nano-QuIC.
papers.abstract: Early diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) is critical, as clinical symptoms typically emerge only after substantial neuronal loss. While α-synuclein (α-Syn) oligomers in blood are promising biomarkers for early detection, their clinical utility is limited by their low abundance and the presence of inhibitory components in the plasma matrix. To address these limitations, we tailored the Nanoparticle-enhanced Quaking-Induced Conversion (Nano-QuIC) platform specifically for the ultrasensitive detection of α-Syn oligomers in human plasma. We identified critical reaction determinants by investigating buffer pH, ionic strength, detergent types, and shaking conditions. Furthermore, the integration of silica nanoparticles (siNPs) proved essential in mitigating plasma matrix interference, ensuring robust and reproducible protein aggregation. Under these optimized conditions, the assay achieved a detection limit of 100 pg/mL for α-Syn oligomers spiked into human plasma. These results demonstrate that our adapted Nano-QuIC platform provides a highly sensitive and minimally invasive method for detecting pathological α-Syn species, offering a significant advancement toward the development of early-stage PD diagnostics.

papers.title: The world smells different in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Olfactory decline is an early sign of Parkinson's disease (PD), often preceding motor symptoms by years to decades. However, because olfactory impairment is also common in healthy and diseased aging, current olfactory performance tests (odor detection, discrimination, and identification) lack disease specificity. In contrast to performance scores, odor-rating-derived olfactory perceptual fingerprints provide a stable measure of how the world smells to an individual. Here, we combine such fingerprints with odor-evoked sniff-response behavior to define an olfactory perceptual-motor signature. To test the hypothesis that this provides a disease-specific marker, we obtained such signatures in three cohorts: Individuals with PD (n = 33), healthy age-matched controls (n = 33), and critically, in participants with non-PD olfactory dysfunction (n = 28). Consistent with previous results, a standard clinical olfactory test detected impairment in both PD and non-PD olfactory dysfunction, but failed to distinguish between these two groups. In contrast, the olfactory perceptual-motor signature both detected impairment and classified PD from non-PD olfactory dysfunction at 94% accuracy (SVM classification, leave-one-out cross-validation, 100% sensitivity, 88% specificity, P = 0.0047). These results dovetail with evidence from vision and audition, implying a perceptual shift rather than only a perceptual decline in PD, and point to the olfactory perceptual-motor signature as a possible disease-specific marker.

papers.title: Differential effects of α-synuclein aggregates on the electrophysiology of SNpc vs VTA dopaminergic neurons in acute mouse slices.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterised by the early loss of dopaminergic neurons (DNs) in substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) with other DNs more resistant. Aggregation of alpha synuclein (α-Syn) appears to be a major driver of pathology. We have investigated the differential effects of intracellular α-Syn aggregates on the electrophysiology of SNpc and VTA DNs in acute slices. Introduction of α-Syn aggregates into single SNpc DNs increased whole-cell conductance and altered firing, effects partially reversed by the KATP

papers.title: A multimodal consensus parcellation of the human brainstem and its applications in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: The brainstem is a highly conserved integrative hub that is essential for arousal, emotion, and motor control, which are functions profoundly affected in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, low signal-to-noise ratios in neuroimaging of subcortical nuclei hinder the construction of brainstem parcellations that integrate complementary functional and structural information, limiting our understanding of circuit-specific pathology. Here, we developed the Multimodal Consensus Brainstem Parcellation (MCBP), a fine-grained atlas that integrates high-resolution naturalistic 7 T functional MRI and diffusion MRI acquired in the Human Connectome Project (N = 160). The MCBP exhibits high reproducibility, symmetry, and homogeneity. Using this parcellation, we find a pronounced structure-function dissociation within the brainstem. Furthermore, MCBP reveals a hierarchical brainstem organization aligned with the unimodal-to-transmodal axis, distinguishing motor execution from visually guided motor preparation that closely resembles the Somato-Cognitive Action Network (SCAN). Crucially, in an independent PD cohort, MCBP-derived connectivity improved disease classification and symptom-severity prediction compared with existing brainstem atlases, supporting its sensitivity to both categorical disease status and dimensional clinical variation. Feature decoding revealed a dual-system pattern of PD-related alterations across sensorimotor and cognitive-affective networks. Notably, it identified a specific brainstem-limbic circuit linked to emotional heterogeneity, providing circuit-level insights for distinguishing anxiety- and depression-related neuropsychiatric PD subtypes independent of motor severity. Beyond distinguishing and grading disease, the MCBP-derived connectivity measure also outperformed those derived from existing atlases in predicting multidimensional behavioral traits in a large healthy participant cohort (N = 976). Gut microbiota and short-chain fatty acids in idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder and Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Idiopathic rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) is a prodromal stage of Parkinson's disease (PD). This study aimed to investigate whether gut microbiota and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) show consistent alterations in iRBD and PD with RBD patients. METHODS: We enrolled 29 iRBD, 24 PD with RBD, 17 PD without RBD, and 18 normal controls (NC). Fecal microbiota composition was analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing, and SCFA concentrations via gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). Clinical symptoms were assessed using motor and non-motor scales, and Spearman correlation analysis was performed to explore interrelationships. papers.title: Anthropometry with a nutritional focus on motor function, hand-grip strength and subjectively assessed fatigue at diagnosis in Parkinson´s disease.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Altered anthropometry and nutritional status are associated with motor- and non-motor symptoms in patients with Parkinson´s disease (PD). OBJECTIVES: To investigate if anthropometry can discriminate between low and high levels of motor symptoms, hand grip strength (HGS) and fatigue. METHODS: Cross-sectional study including baseline data on newly diagnosed patients with PD prior to start of anti-Parkinson medication. Assessments of body composition, risk for malnutrition, fatigue severity scale (FSS) and motor symptoms using Unified Parkinson´s Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS III), including gait performance and ability to arise from chair and HGS were performed at diagnosis. Clinical characteristics and anthropometrical variables were compared between patients with or without motor symptoms and low or high level of fatigue or HGS. Logistic regression was used to examine the association between anthropometry and the odds of having motor difficulties or fatigue. RESULTS: Increased body mass index (BMI) was associated with difficulty arising from chair (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.09, 1.72, p = 0.007). In addition, these patients had low intracellular water index, (5.2 (1.2) vs. 6.4 (0.7) p < 0.001) and fat free mass index (13.9 (2.3) vs. 15.8 (3.1), p = 0.005) and higher fat mass % (42.5 (7.2) vs. 40.2 (9.8), p = 0.024) compared with patients without difficulty. Patients with high FSS had higher UPDRS II (10 (4) vs. 8 (5), p < 0.001), higher BMI (27.9 (3.8) vs. 25.4 (5.7), p = 0.039) and larger calf circumference​ (37.5 (5.0) vs. 35.8 (4.1)), p = 0.045) than patients with low FSS. Low HGS was associated with low mid upper arm circumference (30.0 (4.0) vs. 32.0 (4.0), p < 0.007) and low calf circumference (35.5 (4.4) vs. 37.0 (4.8), p = 0.049), low fat free mass index (14.9 (3.1) vs. 16.0 (3.2)), intracellular water index (5.7 (1.7) vs. 6.4 (1.6), p = 0.004) and arm muscle area (25.5 (3.5) vs. 26.7 (4.3), p = 0.047) as compared with patients with high

papers.title: Serum clusterin, neurofilament light chain, and LDL-C cholesterol for risk stratification of cognitive impairment in parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Serum biomarkers, due to their advantages of easy accessibility and repeatability, show significant potential for early identification and stratification of cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease (PD). OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to systematically evaluate the expression differences of serum clusterin (CLU), neurofilament light chain (NFL), and LDL-C levels in PD patients with different cognitive statuses through a retrospective analysis. METHODS: 90 patients with primary clinically established PD, diagnosed between January 2025 and February 2026, were retrospectively enrolled and stratified by cognitive status into PD with normal cognition (PD-NC), mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI), and dementia (PDD). 90 healthy individuals from the same period served as controls. Fasting venous blood was collected from all subjects to analyze serum levels of CLU, NFL, and LDL-C. Clinical data, including demographics, disease duration, Hoehn-Yahr stage, UPDRS-III, and MoCA scores, were also recorded. Correlation analysis was performed using Spearman's test. A binary logistic regression model was developed for risk prediction, and ROC curves were plotted to evaluate the diagnostic performance of individual biomarkers and the combined model. RESULTS: Serum CLU and NFL levels were significantly higher in the PD group than in healthy controls (P < 0.001), increasing progressively across PD-NC, PD-MCI, and PDD. Conversely, LDL-C levels were significantly lower (P < 0.001), showing an opposite decreasing trend. CLU and NFL correlated negatively with MoCA score, and positively with UPDRS-III scores, while LDL-C showed the reverse pattern (all P < 0.001). A predictive model incorporating Hoehn-Yahr stage, UPDRS-III score, and serum CLU, NFL, and LDL-C levels excellently discriminated PD cognitive impairment (AUC = 0.921). papers.title: Extracellular Vesicle Derived Biomarkers for the Diagnosis of Neurodegenerative Diseases.
papers.abstract: Liquid biopsy, a noninvasive method analyzing biofluids such as blood and cerebrospinal fluid, has transformed early detection and monitoring of neurodegenerative diseases. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) (30-150 nm) secreted by cells are pivotal because of their ability to cross the blood-brain barrier and carry disease-specific cargos like proteins and microRNAs. This review synthesizes recent advancements in EV-based liquid biopsy for diagnosing NDDs, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and frontotemporal dementia. Following PRISMA guidelines, we analyzed 113 studies from databases like PubMed and Scopus, highlighting EV-associated biomarkers' diagnostic potential. These vesicles offer a minimally invasive approach to detect proteinopathies and genetic markers, reflecting central nervous system pathology. Despite their promise, challenges such as standardized isolation protocols and clinical validation remain. This review discusses current trends, methodologies, and future directions for integrating EV-based diagnostics into clinical practice, emphasizing precision medicine for NDDs.

papers.title: SoniNet: an AI framework for enhancing voice features in speech-based health monitoring.
papers.abstract: Deep learning based speech embeddings learned from large-scale speech corpora have achieved strong performance across a range of speech analysis tasks. However, handcrafted acoustic features, such as prosodic, spectral, and voice-quality descriptors, remain widely used in clinical speech analysis because of their established role in characterizing vocal behavior. Despite this, these features often struggle to generalize across variations in speech dynamics, recording duration, and recording conditions. This paper introduces SoniNet

papers.title: Preserved olfaction unmasks choroid plexus-related cognitive risk in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Choroid plexus volume (CPV) has been associated with cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease (PD), particularly frontal-executive dysfunction, whereas olfactory dysfunction is linked to cognitive deterioration and may reflect greater α-synuclein involvement. Whether olfactory status modifies the association between CPV and cognitive outcomes remains unclear. METHODS: We analyzed 718 participants with early-stage PD followed for up to 10 years. Baseline CPV was derived from structural MRI. Hyposmia was defined as an age- and sex-adjusted University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test percentile ≤ 15. Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox models were used to examine incident cognitive milestone (CogM), including a CPV × olfactory status interaction. CPV was standardized to 1-SD units. Multiple sensitivity analyses assessed robustness. RESULTS: Among 709 participants with olfactory data, 502 (70.8%) had hyposmia. Ten-year CogM-free survival was 59.4%. The primary Cox analysis included 680 participants and 173 CogM events. Among participants with normosmia, each 1-SD increase in CPV was associated with higher CogM risk (HR = 1.63, 95% CI 1.20-2.22, P CONCLUSION: Olfactory status modified the association between CPV and cognitive outcomes in early PD. Larger CPV was associated with higher CogM risk in participants with preserved olfaction, but not in those with hyposmia. These findings warrant validation in independent cohorts.

papers.title: Disulfidptosis in neurological disorders: from disulfide stress to actin cytoskeletal collapse.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms driving irreversible neural cell loss in neurodegenerative diseases remain elusive. The collapse of cellular redox balance has unveiled a complex network of emerging metabolic cell death modalities that extend far beyond classical apoptosis. Disulfidptosis, a newly identified form of regulated cell death driven by disulfide stress and uniquely marked by actin cytoskeletal collapse, adds a critical dimension to this network. This review establishes an integrative framework-from sulfur metabolic imbalance to cytoskeletal collapse-for understanding this lethal pathway specifically within the nervous system. we focus on three features that are distinctive to neural tissue: the neuron-glia metabolic coupling that dictates which cell type is most vulnerable; the contrast between chronic disulfide stress dynamics in neurodegeneration and acute stress dynamics in ischemic stroke; and the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and cellular heterogeneity constraints that shape translational strategies. We first establish the cystine/cysteine cycle as the central hub of sulfur metabolism, revealing how it transforms from an antioxidant defense into a lethal driver of disulfide stress upon crossing a critical threshold. We then systematically dissect the molecular machinery of disulfidptosis, centered on NADPH depletion, the SLC7A11 bidirectional paradox, and aberrant cytoskeletal crosslinking. By systematically comparing disulfidptosis with ferroptosis and cuproptosis, we identify the SLC7A11-cystine-NADPH axis as a shared regulatory node. We further discuss how this mechanism may converge to contribute to neural cell injury across chronic neurodegenerative and acute neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, and may also extend to acute neurological conditions such as ischemic stroke. Finally, we propose a dual neuroprotective strategy targeting disulfidptosis and highlight its biomarker potential. Collectively, this review offers a new

papers.title: GPR37 and GPR37L1-mediated neuroprotection: mechanisms and drug repurposing strategies for reducing neurological disorders.
papers.abstract: Neurological disorders such as Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, ischemic stroke, and neuropathic pain are major causes of long-term disability worldwide. The orphan G protein-coupled receptors GPR37 and GPR37L1 have gained considerable research attention as novel therapeutic targets. These receptors play critical roles in neuroprotection, neuroinflammation and tissue repair. GPR37 is primarily expressed in dopaminergic neurons and oligodendrocytes, whereas GPR37L1 is mainly expressed in astrocytes. These receptors modulate various cellular processes through Gi/o-coupled signaling, ERK/MAPK, and PI3K-Akt pathways. Both GPR37 and GPR37L1 affect neuronal survival, remyelination, oxidative stress, apoptosis, glial activation, and phagocytic clearance. Activation of GPR37 and GPR37L1 by their ligands, including prosaposin-derived peptides, neuroprotectin D1, and osteocalcin, regulates protective signaling and promotes functional recovery in the injured central nervous system. This review highlights recent progress in the cellular mechanisms regulating neuroprotection mediated by GPR37 and GPR37L1. This includes GPR37/GPR37L1 molecular characteristics and ligand signaling, mechanisms of proteostasis, ER stress, anti-apoptotic and survival signaling, modulation of oxidative stress, regulation of neuroinflammation, glial-mediated repair and remyelination, and synaptic and dopaminergic regulation. In addition, repurposed drugs targeting these receptors are also reviewed, along with a discussion on the clinical implications of GPR37/GPR37L1 in reducing neurological disorders. Despite these advances, a unified mechanistic framework linking receptor biology with therapeutic development remains lacking. This review proposes a conceptual framework that integrates receptor signaling, disease mechanisms, and drug repurposing strategies, while highlighting testable hypotheses on convergent neuroprotective pathways that warrant experimental validation. papers.title: Thickness of the peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer and its association with disease severity in Parkinson's disease: a cross-sectional case-control study.
papers.abstract: Peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (pRNFL) alterations are linked to retinal neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease (PD), but their regional pattern and clinical relevance remain unclear. This cross-sectional case-control study included 63 PD patients (123 eyes; Hoehn-Yahr [H-Y] stages 1.0-2.5: 47; stages 3-5: 16) and 16 healthy controls (32 eyes). Swept-source optical coherence tomography measured average and quadrant-specific pRNFL thickness. Generalized estimating equations accounted for inter-eye correlation; Benjamini-Hochberg correction controlled the false discovery rate (FDR) within each retinal parameter. Mean pRNFL thickness (prespecified primary outcome) was lower in PD than in controls (107.3 ± 10.9 vs. 112.8 ± 9.4 μm; p = 0.022). The age- and sex-adjusted difference persisted (-6.76 μm; p = 0.005), whereas the moderate-to-advanced versus early-stage difference was nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction (p = 0.148). Temporal pRNFL was thinner (exploratory, unadjusted p = 0.010). In unadjusted models, mean pRNFL thickness was negatively associated with H-Y stage, disease duration, and MDS-UPDRS total, Part II, and Part III scores (all q < 0.01). These associations persisted after adjustment, as did associations of inferior and temporal pRNFL with motor scores (all q < 0.05). No non-motor associations survived FDR correction. Exploratory participant-level ROC analyses yielded AUCs of 0.717 for H-Y stage ≥ 3 (mean pRNFL), 0.727 for MDS-UPDRS Part III ≥ 40 (temporal pRNFL), and 0.681 for PD versus controls (temporal pRNFL). These exploratory findings suggest regionally heterogeneous pRNFL involvement and support pRNFL as a non-invasive candidate marker of retinal neurodegeneration and clinical severity, but not a stand-alone diagnostic biomarker.

papers.title: Updates in Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Behavior Disorder.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia characterized by dream enactment behaviors resulting from loss of normal REM sleep atonia. Increasingly, RBD is recognized not only as a sleep disorder but as a critical neurologic entity, strongly associated with α-synuclein-related neurodegenerative diseases This review highlights recent advances in the understanding of RBD across its clinical spectrum, diagnosis, pathophysiology, and emerging role as a biomarker of neurodegeneration. Current management focuses on safety and symptomatic control, while ongoing research explores disease-modifying therapies and positions RBD as a key platform for neuroprotective clinical trials.

papers.title: Extracellular vesicle-mediated neuroimmune remodeling across synucleinopathies: Therapeutic implications of cell-type specificity and central-peripheral crosstalk.
papers.abstract: Synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy, are characterized by convergent α-synuclein misfolding, impaired proteostasis, and chronic neuroinflammation. Despite these shared pathological features, these disorders exhibit distinct inclusion-bearing cell profiles, vulnerable neural circuits, immune phenotypes, and clinical progression rates, with neuronal inclusions dominating in Parkinson's disease/dementia with Lewy bodies and oligodendrocyte pathology predominating in multiple system atrophy. Extracellular vesicles have emerged as critical modulators integrating these multifaceted pathogenic processes. Secreted by neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, extracellular vesicles cross biological boundaries to deliver diverse bioactive molecules and mediate intercellular communication. This review synthesizes current evidence to propose that extracellular vesicles serve as context-dependent mediators connecting intracellular proteostatic stress to local glial reactivity and systemic immune regulation. Extracellular vesicle-associated α-synuclein maintains a seeding-competent conformation, enters recipient cells, and triggers templated aggregation and inflammatory signaling, although its exact pathogenic contribution relative to free α-synuclein and non-vesicular transmission routes remains undefined. Extracellular vesicle cargo dynamically reshapes microglial and astrocytic activation, oligodendroglial homeostasis, neuronal survival, blood-brain barrier integrity, and peripheral immune recruitment. Extracellular vesicles exert bidirectional effects: pathological extracellular vesicles amplify neurotoxicity, while homeostatic or engineered extracellular vesicles restore proteostasis, optimize immune homeostasis, and facilitate neural tissue repair. papers.title: Editorial: Biomarkers for early detection and progression of Parkinson's disease: integrating genomic, proteomic, imaging, and clinical advances.
Sleep and Neurodegenerative Diseases: Understanding the Bidirectional Relationship.
papers.abstract: Sleep and circadian rhythm disturbances are pervasive across the spectrum of Lewy body disorders (LBDs), including Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. Accumulating clinical, epidemiologic, and neurobiological evidence supports a bidirectional relationship between sleep dysfunction and neurodegeneration, in which pathologic processes disrupt sleep-wake regulation, and impaired sleep may exacerbate neurodegenerative mechanisms, including impaired proteostasis, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and failure of glymphatic clearance. In this review article, the authors synthesize evidence linking sleep and circadian disturbances with LBDs across prodromal, early, and advanced disease stages.

papers.title: Age-conditioned nanomedicine for Parkinson's disease: Pharmaceutical design, brain exposure and regenerative repair.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is predominantly a disorder of older adults, yet nanomedicine studies often optimize carrier performance in young models and use blood-brain barrier (BBB) crossing as the principal success criterion. This mini-review reframes PD nanomedicine as an age-conditioned pharmaceutical design problem in which formulation attributes, route of administration, biological identity, regional exposure, active-payload release, and clearance are jointly determined by the host. Age-related neurovascular remodeling, altered endothelial transport, microglial priming, reduced interstitial and glymphatic clearance, and changes in protein-corona formation are evaluated as variables that can modify both efficacy and safety. Lipid and polymer nanoparticles, drug nanocrystals, intranasal systems, alginate and chitosan formulations, hydrogels, biomimetic carriers, catalytic nanozymes, graphene, and carbon-nanotube interfaces are compared according to the formulation bottleneck they address. Particular attention is given to dopamine stabilization, alpha-synuclein inhibitors and gene-silencing cargo, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory nanozymes, and biomaterial-assisted dopaminergic regeneration. Across platforms, the key pharmaceutical requirement is to connect a critical material attribute to intact-carrier exposure, release of active drug at the relevant site, proximal target engagement, and route-specific safety. A concise translational framework is proposed that combines age-relevant models with critical quality attributes, washout and clearance studies, repeated-dose safety, and manufacturability. Treating aging as a design variable rather than a demographic descriptor should improve the relevance of preclinical formulation development for PD.

papers.title: Clinical application of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and transcranial direct current stimulation as treatment in motor disorders.
papers.abstract: This review examines the potential of the two main noninvasive brain stimulation (NIBS) techniques - repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) - for the treatment of motor disorders. Although rTMS has demonstrated its ability to induce significant changes in various motor and nonmotor symptoms of Parkinson disease (PD), its clinical application remains limited, except for the treatment of PD-associated depression using rTMS applied to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Some theoretical concepts support the use of certain "excitability-decreasing" NIBS protocols (rTMS delivered at low frequency or as continuous θ burst stimulation (cTBS), or cathodal tDCS) applied to motor cortical regions to alleviate dystonia. Similarly, "excitability-decreasing" NIBS protocols, but applied to the cerebellum, have shown some beneficial effects on various forms of ataxia or tremor. On the other hand, the use of anodal tDCS of the cerebellum combined with cathodal spinal DCS is a particularly promising prospect, as well as closed-loop transcranial alternating current stimulation protocols on tremor. In the context of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, NIBS techniques aim to promote neuroprotection, at least in the early stages of the disease. This can be achieved by applying cTBS or anodal tDCS (possibly combined with cathodal spinal DCS) to motor cortical regions. However, the clinical relevance of NIBS techniques is generally limited by the short-lived nature of their effects, requiring repeated sessions, particularly for rTMS, which may not be an optimal care model in the context of highly chronic conditions such as motor disorders. Therefore, home-based tDCS could open new avenues for the clinical application of NIBS, thanks to its ease of use and lower rate of adverse effects compared to invasive neuromodulation methods or surgical lesions. papers.title: Polypharmacy and the ageing brain: Anticholinergic burden in the ageing population and the impact of gynaecological medications.
papers.journal: European journal of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive biology
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Population ageing is accelerating worldwide, with increasing multimorbidity and polypharmacy. Medicines with anticholinergic properties are widely prescribed in older adults for conditions, including depression, urinary incontinence, Parkinson's disease, allergies, and respiratory disorders. While short-term anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth and constipation are well recognised, increasing evidence suggests that cumulative anticholinergic exposure may contribute to adverse cognitive outcomes. OBJECTIVE: This review discusses the concept of anticholinergic burden, outlines commonly used tools to quantify exposure, and examines the evidence linking cumulative anticholinergic exposure with cognitive decline and other adverse health outcomes. It also explores strategies to identify and mitigate anticholinergic burden in clinical practice. METHODS: Relevant literature on anticholinergic medications, burden scales, and associated clinical outcomes was reviewed. Attention was given to studies assessing cognitive and functional outcomes and to validated tools, including the Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden (ACB) scale, Anticholinergic Risk Scale (ARS), and Anticholinergic Drug Scale (ADS). RESULTS: Observational studies have reported associations between higher cumulative anticholinergic burden and adverse outcomes including cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, and functional decline. However, findings regarding long-term cognitive decline and dementia remain inconsistent and vary according to drug class and the burden scale used. Anticholinergic burden tools can support identification of cumulative medication exposure, but their scores should not be interpreted as precise measures of individual cognitive risk. CONCLUSION: Although the evidence linking cumulative anticholinergic exposure with long-term cognitive decline and dementia remains inconsistent and predominantly observational, higher anticholinergic burden has been associated with adverse outc

papers.title: Factor Structure, Reliability, and Validity of the Beck Depression Inventory-II in Older Adults With Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Depression is among the most common nonmotor manifestations of Parkinson's disease (PD) and substantially contributes to reduced quality of life and functional impairment. Despite the widespread use of the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) in PD, evidence regarding its dimensional structure and construct validity in older adults remains limited. This study aimed to investigate the structural validity, reliability, and construct validity of the BDI-II in older adults with PD. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, 190 older adults with PD and 95 age-matched healthy controls were enrolled. Participants with PD completed the BDI-II, the Geriatric Depression Scale-15 (GDS-15), the depression and anxiety subscales of the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS-D and HADS-A), and the Parkinson Anxiety Scale (PAS). Structural validity was examined using exploratory factor analysis. Internal consistency, test-retest reliability, convergent validity, discriminant validity, and known-groups validity were also evaluated. RESULTS: Exploratory factor analysis suggested a preliminary three-factor structure of the Persian BDI-II. The BDI-II demonstrated excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α CONCLUSIONS: The BDI-II demonstrated high internal consistency, excellent short-term test-retest reliability, and preliminary evidence of convergent construct validity in this selected sample of older adults with PD. The findings provide preliminary support for assessing depressive symptom severity, while further studies using independent samples, confirmatory factor analysis, structured diagnostic assessment, and longitudinal psychometric approaches are required to establish its broader clinical applicability.

papers.title: Persistent Hypersomnia in Neurological Disease: Mechanisms, Diagnosis, and Management.
papers.abstract: Hypersomnia in neurological disease is characterized by excessive sleep quantity in a day, distinct from excessive daytime sleepiness. It arises from the disruption of brainstem-hypothalamic-thalamic arousal circuits and neurotransmitter systems. Hypersomnia significantly impacts quality of life, safety, cognition, rehabilitation, and caregiver burden across conditions, including Parkinson's disease, stroke, traumatic brain injury, and multiple sclerosis. Systematic evaluation with polysomnography/multiple sleep latency testing distinguishes hypersomnia from fatigue and apathy. Treatment involves mechanism-guided approaches: addressing reversible causes (medications, sleep disorders), then pharmacotherapy with wake-promoting agents or stimulants, with special considerations for epilepsy, autonomic dysfunction, and neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Clinical applications of ultrasound neuromodulation of the motor system.
papers.abstract: Ultrasound-based neuromodulation includes magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound and low-intensity transcranial ultrasound stimulation. Both utilize acoustic energy to reach deep brain structures with high spatial precision through the intact skull. Magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound produces precise thermal ablation, whereas transcranial ultrasound stimulation uses low-intensity, pulsed sonication to reversibly modulate neuronal excitability without tissue damage. This chapter reviews their methodological principles, mechanisms of action, and clinical applications of ultrasound in motor system disorders. Magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound is an approved incisionless alternative to surgical lesion or deep brain stimulation for treatment of essential tremor and Parkinson disease, with accurate lesioning of thalamic and pallidal targets under MRI guidance. Transcranial ultrasound stimulation, in contrast, is at an earlier translational stage, with preclinical and early clinical studies that demonstrated safe, bidirectional modulation of cortical and subcortical circuits, and potential for improvement in motor functions in Parkinson disease, tremor, and poststroke recovery. Together, these modalities represent a therapeutic continuum spanning permanent ablation to reversible neuromodulation and highlight the role of ultrasound neuromodulation as both a research and clinical tool in movement disorders and motor system disorders.

papers.title: Clinical applications of brain-computer interfaces in the motor system.
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable direct interaction between neural activity and external devices or neuromodulatory systems, offering novel approaches for restoring, rehabilitating, and modulating motor function following neurologic injury and disease. Over recent decades, BCIs have progressed from experimental demonstrations of operant conditioning to clinically relevant technologies applied in stroke, spinal cord injury, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, movement disorders, and other motor syndromes. This chapter presents a critical, clinically focused review of motor BCIs, with emphasis on clinical applications rather than technical fundamentals. Key topics include invasive and noninvasive signal acquisition methods, anatomic targets for recording and stimulation, decoding and artificial intelligence approaches, and actuator systems such as robotics, functional electrical stimulation, and spinal or cortical neuromodulation. Particular attention is directed toward hybrid and closed-loop architectures that connect motor intention with sensory or motor outcomes through precise temporal contingency, a fundamental requirement for promoting adaptive neuroplasticity. Evidence from randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, and emerging invasive studies is evaluated, highlighting areas with substantial clinical support, particularly poststroke motor rehabilitation and adaptive deep brain stimulation for Parkinson disease, as well as fields undergoing active translational development. The chapter also addresses efficacy measures, treatment durability, and current barriers to widespread clinical implementation, while outlining future directions involving minimally invasive implants, adaptive decoders, and network-level neuromodulation.

papers.title: Ventral tegmental area dopaminergic neurons contribute to hindlimb control during obstacle-avoidance locomotion in mice.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Dopamine neurons in the midbrain contribute to motor, cognitive and memory functions, and their degeneration has been implicated in gait instability and increased fall risk during obstacle-avoidance behavior. However, the specific contribution of ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopaminergic neurons to visually guided locomotion remains poorly understood. METHODS: We examined obstacle-avoidance locomotion in mice that received bilateral injections of either 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) or saline into the VTA. High-speed motion-capture analysis was used to evaluate obstacle-contact frequency, limb kinematics, and forelimb-hindlimb coordination. RESULTS: Compared with the saline-injected control group, the 6-OHDA lesion group exhibited a higher frequency of contacts by the leading hindlimb, including both stomps and grazes. Stomping was associated with impaired adjustment of stride length and landing position, whereas grazing occurrence was unrelated to takeoff position. In addition, the leading hindlimb in the lesion group initiated toe elevation earlier during obstacle negotiation, a change not observed during overground locomotion. Furthermore, the lesion group exhibited greater forelimb-hindlimb distance immediately before obstacle crossing, suggesting impaired interlimb coordination. DISCUSSION: Collectively, these findings suggest that VTA dopamine neurons contribute to memory-guided control of the leading hindlimb during obstacle negotiation. These results may provide insight into mechanisms underlying altered obstacle negotiation in patients with Parkinson's disease.

papers.title: Preliminary evidence on the validity and reliability of the Trail Walking Test for assessing complex walking in people with Parkinson's disease.
papers.journal: International journal of rehabilitation research. Internationale Zeitschrift fur Rehabilitationsforschung. Revue internationale de recherches de readaptation
papers.abstract: The Trail Walking Test (TWT) assesses complex walking through visual scanning, sequential target identification, and repeated directional changes. This study investigated its test-retest reliability and preliminary validity in people with Parkinson's disease. Thirty-four people with Parkinson's disease participated in this cross-sectional methodological study. Test-retest reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), SEM, and minimal detectable change at the 95% confidence level (MDC95). Convergent validity was examined through correlations with clinical measures. Known-groups validity was assessed according to fall history and freezing of gait (FoG) status. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were exploratory. The TWT demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability [ICC = 0.955, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.911-0.977], with an SEM of 5.0 s and MDC95 of 13.8 s. TWT completion time was strongly correlated with motor symptom severity (r = 0.844), FoG severity (r = 0.833), Trail Making Test Part A performance (r = 0.808), and cognitive-motor interference during the Timed Up and Go Test (r = 0.756). Completion time was longer in participants with a history of falls and those classified as freezers (both P < 0.001). Exploratory ROC analyses yielded area under the curve of 0.911 (95% CI: 0.816-1.000) for fall history and 0.937 (95% CI: 0.862-1.000) for FoG status. These preliminary findings support the reliability and provide initial evidence of the validity of the TWT in people with Parkinson's disease. The TWT may provide complementary information about complex walking performance. The ROC findings should be interpreted cautiously and require confirmation in larger, independent samples before clinical application can be considered.

papers.title: Enjoyment and engagement during virtual reality and active video gaming rehab in individuals with Parkinson disease: a systematic scoping review.
papers.abstract: AIM: To systematically review the literature to identify, examine, and summarise the role of enjoyment and engagement and how these are measured during virtual reality (VR)/active video gaming (AVG) intervention in patients with Parkinson Disease (PD). METHOD: A systematic search was conducted across 7 electronic databases: PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, PsycINFO, Cochrane, EMBASE, and IEEE Xplore from January 2000 to August 2026. To be included, studies had to include people with PD, have VR/AVG as the intervention, and include enjoyment and/or engagement as the outcome. RESULTS: 2348 articles were screened, and 10 studies were included in this review: 3 used AVG, 6 used VR systems and 1 used an AR system as intervention programs for 338 participants with PD; ranging in age from 52-90 years. Study quality ranged from fair to good, with varying degrees of enjoyment and/or engagement reported with VR/AVG interventions in PD. CONCLUSION: When measured, interventions involving VR/AVG may be enjoyable and engaging for adults with PD. Future studies using AVG/VR need to measure these constructs comprehensively using well validated measures to build a stronger evidence base for clinicians to use these interventions to provide an engaging and enjoyable form of exercise.

papers.title: Satisfaction with hospital-based outpatient rehabilitation in people with Parkinson's disease and its association with life satisfaction and health-related quality of life: a longitudinal national register study.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To examine satisfaction with hospital-based outpatient rehabilitation and its association with life satisfaction and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in people with Parkinson's disease, and whether sex and age affect possible associations. DESIGN: A longitudinal national register study.  Methods: Data from the Swedish register for rehabilitation medicine included 173 individuals with Parkinson's disease. Self-reported questionnaires were collected at admission, discharge, and 1-year follow-up. Associations between satisfaction with rehabilitation received (register-based questionnaire) and life satisfaction (Life Satisfaction Questionnaire, LiSat-11 global item) and HRQoL (EuroQol 5 dimensions questionnaire, EQ5D) were examined using regression analyses. RESULTS: Over 82% of the participants were satisfied with the outpatient rehabilitation on discharge. High satisfaction with several aspects of rehabilitation was associated with higher scores on LiSat-11 and EQ-5D at discharge, whereas few associations were observed at the 1-year follow-up. Men and older adults (> 69 years) demonstrated broader associations than women and younger adults. CONCLUSION: Greater satisfaction with hospital-based outpatient rehabilitation was associated with higher life satisfaction and HRQoL on discharge, whereas these associations were less evident at the 1-year follow-up. Assessing patients' experiences of rehabilitation and patient-reported outcome measures may provide complementary perspectives when evaluating and developing rehabilitation in people with Parkinson's disease.

papers.title: Inhibitors of Gut Bacterial l-Dopa Decarboxylation with Reduced Susceptibility to Host Metabolism.
papers.abstract: Microorganisms in the human gut influence the efficacy and metabolism of host-targeted small molecule therapeutics, including the frontline Parkinson's disease drug levodopa (l-dopa). Previous work has identified a mechanism-based inhibitor of gut bacterial decarboxylases that degrade l-dopa, α-fluoromethyltyrosine (AFMT). However, early experiments with AFMT in rodent models suggested undesirable in vivo metabolism by host tyrosine hydroxylase, producing α-fluoromethyldopa, a metabolite likely to worsen Parkinson's phenotypes and prevent application as an l-dopa cotreatment. Here, we demonstrate oxidation of AFMT to α-fluoromethyldopa in vitro by recombinant human tyrosine hydroxylase. We then develop AFMT analogues that retain activity against bacterial decarboxylases but have reduced susceptibility to host hydroxylation. Suitable arenes for inhibitor design were identified using assays with commercially available noncanonical amino acids, which revealed aryl difluorination as a promising modification. Difluoroaryl AFMT derivatives are less prone to degradation by tyrosine hydroxylase in vitro yet still inhibit l-dopa metabolism by bacterial decarboxylases. This work exemplifies how substrate reactivity can streamline design of mechanism-based enzyme inhibitors, as well as how constraints posed by the host can be incorporated during development of microbiome-targeted therapeutics. The compounds reported here are promising starting points for future studies in animal models and further exploration of gut bacterial effects on l-dopa treatment efficacy.

papers.title: Genome-resolved multi-omics characterizes bacterial, viral, and metabolic components associated with Parkinson's disease gut ecosystem variation.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is increasingly recognized as a disorder involving the gut-brain axis, yet genome-resolved characterization of bacterial and viral communities with metabolic context remains limited. Here, we performed deep shotgun metagenomic sequencing and fecal metabolomic profiling in a high-altitude cohort comprising patients with PD and environmentally matched spouse controls (living at approximately 1,900 m altitude). We reconstructed 455 species-level genome bins (SGBs) and 2,957 non-redundant viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), enabling high-resolution profiling of bacterial and viral community composition. Rather than a uniform shift of the entire microbial community, PD-associated variation involved specific bacterial, viral, and metabolic components. Indicator analysis identified 23 bacterial and 86 viral candidate indicators associated with PD or control status, with predicted temperate phages representing the predominant lifestyle category among indicator vOTUs. Several PD-associated bacterial indicators included taxa previously linked to anaerobic fermentation and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-associated metabolism, accompanied by increased fecal valerate. Abundance correlation analysis identified covariation patterns between bacterial and viral indicators, including associations between controls (CK)-associated Agathobacter faecis

papers.title: Safety and quality of life outcome of trans-anal irrigation for chronic constipation in Parkinson's disease: a pilot study.
papers.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Constipation in Parkinson's Disease (PD) is the main and most disabling non-motor symptom. Laxatives, prebiotics and probiotics are therapeutic options for neurological bowel diseases, and recently, Trans-Anal Irrigation (TAI) has also been considered in poor responders to medical treatment. OBJECTIVE: The primary aim was to evaluate safety and indication of TAI in treating PD constipation. METHODS: A pilot, prospective, observational, cohort study enrolled PD patients with chronic constipation. At baseline, TAI was proposed. Patients who accepted TAI had a neurological and proctological assessment at baseline (T0), 6-month (T1) and 12-month (T2). RESULTS: Twelve patients accepted TAI. At T1 and T2, no side effects were recorded. TAI patients showed statistically improved proctological assessment (p < 0.001) and unchanged neurological scores except for the PDQ-39 questionnaire (p < 0.001) at T2. CONCLUSIONS: TAI is safe for constipation treatment in PD. Improving intestinal transit might ameliorate quality of life, laying the foundation for new therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Clinical neurophysiology studies in the diagnosis of movement disorders.
papers.abstract: Clinical neurophysiology (CNP) tools are increasingly used to diagnose, characterize, and refine the management of movement disorders. This chapter provides an overview of well-established applications of CNP for movement disorders in clinical practice, exploring standardized protocols and criteria for differentiating various movement types. These include illustrative examples for the determination of the location of myoclonus generator, distinguishing between tremor subtypes (e.g., Parkinsonian, essential, and enhanced physiologic tremor), and diagnosis of conditions such as functional movement disorder, stiff-person syndrome, and orthostatic tremor. The chapter also examines emerging applications of CNP tools to differentiate conditions such as dystonia, tics, and chorea, which remain complex and under active investigation. As the field progresses, integrating CNP with other diagnostic tools, such as imaging, genetics, and video recording, has the potential to refine diagnosis, monitor disease progression, and assess treatment response. We hope this chapter will encourage the broader adoption of these techniques in clinical practice.
